meta.title: How This System Was Designed — Technical Considerations

scenes.title: Correctness here is a whole-system property, not a per-screen one
scenes.narration: This is a hospital admissions system. The hard part isn't any single screen. One patient passes through five roles in turn — the emergency department, the specialists, bed management, the ward nurse, housekeeping. Each does its bit and hands the patient to the next. No single role owns whether the final outcome is correct. Correctness is a property of the handoffs between them. So that is the thing I designed for, and everything in this walkthrough is about keeping the whole system correct as the patient moves through it.

scenes.title: The domain is a tree of beds, each in exactly one state
scenes.narration: Before the decisions, here is the model they act on. Five entities in a tree: a level holds wards, and a ward holds beds. A bed is always in exactly one of four states, and it moves between them by legal steps only. Six roles act on that tree, each seeing its own view of the same data. And the system has to talk to three outside systems — patient records, sister hospitals, notifications — none of which I could actually connect to. That last line is the constraint that shapes every decision after this one, so hold on to it.

scenes.title: 02b-bed-board-capture
scenes.narration: Here is that model running. It looks like a dashboard, but underneath it is a state machine. Every button is a legal move from one bed state to the next, and a bed cannot leave one state without entering another — there is no gap it can fall into. That is the first thing correctness rests on: a bed can never quietly go missing, because the only way to change one is a move the system recognises. Now, the five decisions — each one a place this could go wrong, in the order the patient meets them.

scenes.title: The two easy ways to build this both fail
scenes.narration: There are two easy ways to build a prototype like this, and both fail. The first is to fake everything behind a polished interface. On camera, a real safety rule and a fake one look exactly the same, so faking it proves nothing to anyone who understands the domain. The second is to build all of it for real. That never finishes — there is no records endpoint, no identity provider, no solver licence, one engineer, and no production access. So the real decision, before any feature, is where to spend the effort I actually had.

scenes.title: The part you cannot fake
scenes.narration: And the safety-critical part cannot be faked. Put one man in an empty six-bed cubicle, and the other five beds can now only take men. Get a rule like that wrong and the result isn't rough or unpolished — it is simply wrong, and anyone who knows the domain sees it at a glance. So the safety rules had to be real code, not a demo. That single choice decides what got built to production standard and what got stubbed. And it points at the real question the rest of this film answers: correctness here has to hold in five specific places, in the order the patient moves through them. Here is the first.

scenes.title: No bed until every consult is in
scenes.narration: The first place is eligibility — deciding when a patient is even allowed to compete for a bed. A patient who needs specialist input is not put in the bed queue right away. The request is held in a state called ASSESSMENT_PENDING, hidden from bed management, until every specialist consult comes back. And a specialist can chain another consult onto it — which opens a new request that the patient now also waits for. Only when all of them are complete does the request flip to eligible and appear in the queue. The trade-off is honest: entry is slower. But the alternative is allocating a bed before the specialists agree, which means committing a patient the assessment might still change. In this domain, that is the wrong trade, so the gate stays closed.

scenes.title: 05a-consult-hold-capture
scenes.narration: You can watch the gate close in the emergency department view. The doctor picks a patient and sends the case out to specialist clusters. The moment that happens, the admission drops into ASSESSMENT_PENDING and stays there. It will not reach bed management, and no bed can be allocated to it, until the consults resolve. This is the rule stated in the interface, on the way in — but the interface only shows you the happy path, where the consults come back cleanly.

scenes.title: 05b-consensus-gate-terminal
scenes.narration: The part you cannot see in the interface is what happens when the consults come back one at a time — because partial agreement is the case that actually breaks systems. This test completes some of the broadcasts but deliberately not all of them, then checks the request. It is still held. The code only advances the status to bed-requested inside a single check: every broadcast must read COMPLETED. One outstanding consult, and the gate stays shut. Partial agreement is not agreement, and the bed queue never sees the request until the last consult lands.

scenes.title: When specialists disagree, the system takes the safe side
scenes.narration: But the consults that gate is waiting for can disagree — and that is the second place correctness has to hold. Several specialists review the same patient, and they can return different acuity levels and different monitoring needs. The system does not stop and ask a coordinator to settle it. It resolves by construction: it takes the highest acuity anyone assigned, and it turns on every monitoring requirement anyone flagged — the union, not the average. The cost is that it sometimes provisions more than a patient strictly needs. In exchange, a disagreement can never resolve toward the less safe option. When people disagree about safety, the system always rounds up. That is deliberate.

scenes.title: 06a-discordance-terminal
scenes.narration: Here is that rule as code, because the resolution is invisible in the interface. When the consults are reconciled, the effective acuity is set to the highest tier across every respondent, not the emergency department's original number. And the bed queue sorts on that effective tier — so a patient any specialist marked more critical moves up the queue automatically. The test pins it: feed in a higher specialist tier, and the effective tier rises to match. The safe side wins without anyone having to remember to make it win.

scenes.title: The clinical decision and the bed decision have different owners
scenes.narration: Once a consult resolves, the third place is ownership — who is allowed to act on it. Clinicians decide the clinical picture: the acuity, the monitoring, whether to divert. They do not touch the ward or the bed. That is bed management's call, and only after consensus. I split it on purpose. Making a doctor negotiate a ward in the middle of emergency triage creates friction between departments and pulls them off patient care. The cost is one more handoff between roles. The benefit is that each decision is made by the person who should own it, with the information they actually have — and, as the next two takes show, the split isn't just convention, it is enforced.

scenes.title: 07a-admitting-authority-capture
scenes.narration: You can see the split on the queue itself. The blue badge is the admitting cluster the coordinator set — that is the authoritative one. The plain badge next to it is the emergency department's suspected service, its opening guess. The allocation engine scores beds against the coordinator's choice, never the guess. Two different decisions, two different owners, and the system records which one is authoritative rather than blending them.

scenes.title: 07b-authority-enforced-terminal
scenes.narration: And the interface can hide a split that the code doesn't really keep, so here is the proof it does. Tagging an operational delay is a bed-management action. This test tries it twice: once as a bed coordinator, which succeeds, and once as an emergency department attending, which is refused with an access-denied error. The role check lives in the service method, below the interface, so it holds no matter which screen or client calls it. Authority isn't a label on a badge — it is a rule the write path enforces.

scenes.title: 07c-two-tier-safety-terminal
scenes.narration: This is the safety part from earlier, made concrete — and it is the reason bed allocation had to be real code. The rules come in two tiers. Absolute invariants — putting a man in a women's cubicle, or an airborne-infectious patient in a ward with no negative pressure — are rejected outright with an unprocessable-entity error, and there is no override path at all. Operational rules — a ward-class upgrade, a telemetry mismatch — are rejected too, but with a bad-request error the coordinator can override by supplying a structured reason code. Four tests, one allocation method: the things that must never happen cannot be forced, and the things that sometimes should happen require a reason on the record.

scenes.title: Two people can race for the same thing; only one wins
scenes.narration: Once a decision has a clear owner, the fourth place is contention — two owners reaching for the same thing at the same moment. Two specialists can try to claim the same case. Two coordinators can try to allocate the same bed. Only one can win. I used optimistic locking — a version column on the three entities that race — rather than pessimistic locking. The reasoning is the cost of losing. Here, the loser simply gets a conflict, sees the case is already taken, and picks the next one. Nothing is lost. Pessimistic locking would hold a database lock to prevent a conflict that costs nothing and corrects itself, while adding deadlock risk and pressure on the connection pool. So optimistic isn't just the cheaper choice — it is the correct one for this cost structure.

scenes.title: 08a-vacate-capture
scenes.narration: Contention only stays safe if every change is a controlled move, so first, the state machine that guards them. A nurse discharges a patient. The bed does not jump straight to available — it goes to pending cleaning, and a thirty-minute clock starts. There is no path from occupied to clean, because in a real hospital there isn't one. Each move checks the state it is leaving before it makes the change, and refuses if the bed isn't where it expects.

steps.target: Patient Vacated Bed on the first occupied bed

scenes.title: 08a2-sanitise-capture
scenes.narration: Housekeeping signs off the cleaning, and only then does the bed return to the pool as clean. Four states, and every move between them is a guarded step: the method checks the current state, refuses if it is wrong, and writes the next state inside a single database transaction. That is the detail that makes the version column enough. Two people acting on the same bed both read the same starting state, but only the first write commits — the second finds the version has moved and is rejected. The guard defines the legal moves; the version number decides who wins the race for one of them.

scenes.title: 08b-conflict-409-terminal
scenes.narration: The race itself I cannot show honestly in a browser — a real race needs two clients hitting the server at the same instant, and faking it in one tab would be a lie. So it is a test. Two specialists claim the same broadcast. The first write wins. The second comes back as a 409 Conflict, carrying a problem-detail body the client can actually act on, rather than a stack trace. That is the losing writer being told to retry — which, because losing costs nothing here, is exactly the behaviour we want.

scenes.title: Provable where built, loud where not
scenes.narration: The fifth is different in kind. The first four were places in the patient's path; this one is a property about all of them — whether any of it is actually provable, and what happens where I stopped building. Two things. First, every operational metric can be computed two ways, from the database and from the audit log, and a test fails if the two disagree — so the numbers are checked against themselves, not trusted. Second, for the parts I did not build: they sit behind interfaces chosen by a single Spring profile at startup, and the production versions throw the moment they are called instead of returning fake data. The honest cost is that only the prototype side of each boundary is tested. But an unbuilt piece that fails loudly is far safer than one that quietly pretends to work.

scenes.title: 09a-analytics-capture
scenes.narration: This is the first pathway — the metrics read from the database. Twenty of them across four sections, each with a benchmark and whether it was met. These aren't figures typed onto a slide. The running system computed them from the very workflows in this walkthrough, which is why they move when the workflows do.

scenes.title: 09b-parity-terminal
scenes.narration: And the two pathways are checked against each other, not eyeballed. The reconciliation test computes each metric from the database and again from the audit log, and fails if any pair disagrees. That check is the only thing that earns the cost of maintaining a second pathway at all — without it, a second source of numbers is just a second thing that can be wrong.

scenes.title: 09c-stub-contract-terminal
scenes.narration: And the parts I did not build are tested to fail on purpose. The three production adapters — the constraint solver, the records gateway, the transfer gateway — each throw the instant they are invoked. This matters because the quiet failure is the dangerous one: a placeholder that returns plausible fake data eventually gets called by accident, in a profile nobody checked, and no one notices. These cannot. If the wrong profile ever runs them, it stops immediately and says so.

scenes.title: 09d-coverage-capture
scenes.narration: Measured across the whole backend: ninety-four percent of instructions, ninety-seven percent of lines, and sixty-nine percent of branches. The branch number is the one worth saying out loud, because branches are where the untested paths hide. Ninety-four and ninety-seven say the domain layer is well exercised; sixty-nine says there are decision paths I have not covered. It is an honest measurement of what is tested, not a gate that blocks anything.

scenes.title: 09e-gate-red-terminal
scenes.narration: And here is the most honest thing I can show you, because it is a weakness I left in. The frontend declares four coverage thresholds at ninety percent. Run them and one comes back red — branches at about seventy-five. Nothing caught it before now, because nothing runs these thresholds automatically. A threshold that no pipeline runs is not a safeguard; it is a number sitting in a config file. That is on the list of what this prototype still owes, and I would rather name it than hide it.

scenes.title: What's stubbed, and the boundary it's stubbed behind
scenes.narration: So here is everything that is stubbed, gathered in one place, and all of it stubbed on purpose. In-memory data that a restart wipes. Polling instead of real-time push. A heuristic instead of a real constraint solver. Header-driven personas instead of real authentication. And no continuous integration to run the coverage gates. The point is that every one of these already sits behind an interface or a profile that is in place today — so the production version is added behind that boundary, not retrofitted through the code. On method: an AI coding assistant wrote a lot of this code. Which trade-off to make, which approach was right, and the final shape of the design — those decisions were mine.
